strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP deployment problem: preserving safety during benign instruction fine-tuning. The proposed differentiated learning-rate strategy is straightforward to integrate into LoRA training.

The reported improvements over standard IFT are substantial across several models and attack sets. For example, on GPT-3-generated Alpaca data, Llama-2-7B's average attack success rate decreases from 67.57% to 17.57%. Detailed per-attack results make these aggregate gains inspectable.

The experiments include useful supporting checks: comparable synthetic-task accuracy, an earlier standard-IFT checkpoint with comparable training loss, extension to attention and MLP modules, and direct experiments showing that tuning deeper layers causes less safety degradation.
weaknesses: The central security proxy is insufficiently validated. Distinguishing benign from malicious instructions in hidden representations does not establish that a model will refuse harmful requests. Moreover, robustness to zeroing half of a weight matrix need not predict robustness to learned LoRA updates. Section 6.2 provides behavioral support for the layer-depth pattern, but does not establish that proxy scores predict safety across module types or candidate subsets. The claims about identifying security-relevant modules therefore exceed the evidence.

The comparisons do not isolate the value of proxy-guided selection. Missing controls include a tuned uniform learning rate, simply freezing early layers, a fixed late-layer subset, and random subsets with matched adaptation capacity. This matters especially because the general-domain learning rates differ by a factor of 10,000, effectively freezing much of the model. The earlier-checkpoint comparison addresses one underfitting concern, but cannot establish superiority over these simpler alternatives. There are also no empirical comparisons with other safety-preserving fine-tuning methods.

Section 5.2 explicitly selects checkpoints using the same 100 test expressions used to report expertise, with different selection rules for standard IFT and ML-LR. This compromises the held-out interpretation of the task-performance results. A separate validation split and a common selection protocol are needed. Broader expertise claims are also limited by evaluation on one small synthetic operator task; the general-domain experiments actually reduce usability relative to the base models.

Reproducibility and evaluation independence are incomplete. The manuscript omits important classifier-training and fine-tuning details, including optimizer configuration, batch size, schedules, and seeds, and does not provide an accompanying release of the manually edited proxy data or private mathematics dataset. The proxy's Xtest is repeatedly used for module selection, so it functions as validation data. Whether its AdvBench instructions overlap the final safety evaluation is not specified. The attack-generation targets and whether attacks are regenerated against tuned models also need clarification.

No repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or judge-validation results are reported. With only 50–100 examples per attack and 100 task examples, this limits confidence in smaller safety differences and claims of equivalent expertise. The large aggregate improvements are encouraging, but do not resolve these uncertainties.

Some quantitative reporting needs correction: Section 6.1 claims an average ASR reduction of 46.24%, whereas Tables 9–10 imply approximately 34.68 percentage points. Overall, the promising behavioral results warrant further development, but validating the proxy, adding matched controls, and repairing test-based checkpoint selection are important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: preserving safety during benign instruction fine-tuning. The proposed differentiated learning-rate strategy is straightforward to integrate into LoRA training.

The reported improvements over standard fine-tuning are substantial and reasonably consistent across models and evaluation sets. For example, Table 6 reports average ASR reductions from 67.57% to 17.57% for Llama2-7B and from 71.86% to 23.14% for Llama3.1-8B.

The experiments include useful checks beyond the main comparison: an earlier standard-IFT checkpoint with comparable training loss, LoRA targeting all module types, and synthetic task adaptation with similar reported accuracy. The appendix provides detailed per-attack results and search pseudocode.
weaknesses: The central security proxy is insufficiently validated. Accurately classifying malicious versus benign input representations does not establish that a model will refuse harmful requests. Likewise, stability under zeroing half of a weight matrix need not predict safety under gradient-based LoRA updates. The paper does not quantify the relationship between proxy degradation and actual harmful-response rates across module subsets. Section 6.2 supports a coarse depth trend, but does not validate the module ranking or distinguish safety-specific sensitivity from general representational disruption.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of proxy-guided selection. In the general-domain setting, the two learning rates differ by a factor of 10,000, effectively freezing much of the model. Missing controls include uniformly reduced learning rates, simple late-layer tuning, and random or size-matched module subsets. The earlier-checkpoint comparison is useful but does not replace these controls. Comparisons with relevant safety-preserving fine-tuning methods are also absent.

The task-performance evaluation uses the test set for checkpoint selection. Section 5.2 explicitly selects standard-IFT checkpoints by maximum test accuracy and ML-LR checkpoints by matching that accuracy. Consequently, Tables 3–4 do not provide an independent estimate of retained task performance. A separate validation set, a predetermined selection rule, and an untouched test set are needed.

Evidence for practical adaptation is narrow. General-domain fine-tuning decreases usability relative to the base models for both methods, while the sole specific-domain task is a small synthetic operator dataset with 100 test examples. These experiments provide preliminary evidence, but do not establish preservation of useful adaptation across realistic domains. Furthermore, the sampled Alpaca data are treated as entirely benign without a documented audit or filtering procedure, leaving the defining experimental premise insufficiently verified.

Evaluation independence and uncertainty need clarification. The proxy uses AdvBench-derived examples, and downstream evaluation also includes AdvBench, without documenting disjointness. The proxy's Xtest is repeatedly used during module search and therefore functions as validation data. Results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, and the attack setup does not clearly establish whether automated attacks were regenerated against each tuned model. These omissions particularly weaken claims based on smaller differences.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful pseudocode: classifier optimization settings, exact data splits and edited instruction pairs, optimizer and batch settings, decoding configuration, and search costs are not adequately specified. Algorithm 1 also assumes attention-module access and dLLM-based slicing, leaving its adaptation to MLP modules and differently shaped attention projections unclear. There is a numerical reporting error: Tables 9–10 imply an average ASR reduction of approximately 34.68 percentage points, rather than the 46.24% stated in Section 6.1.

Overall, the substantial empirical improvements merit further development, but the unvalidated proxy, missing selection controls, and test-based checkpoint selection prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version. These are concrete methodological revisions that could reasonably be addressed for the next review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: preserving safety during benign instruction fine-tuning while retaining adaptation benefits. The proposed module-specific learning-rate strategy is straightforward to apply with LoRA.

The reported safety improvements are substantial across three Llama models, two general-domain training datasets, and seven attack settings. For example, Table 6 reduces Llama2-7B's average attack success rate from 67.57% to 17.57%. These behavioral evaluations provide meaningful evidence beyond the classifier proxy.

The synthetic operator-learning experiment demonstrates useful adaptation alongside improved safety: Llama2-13B reaches 89% task accuracy with both methods, while average attack success rate decreases from 15.43% to 9.00%.

The paper includes useful additional analyses: an earlier-checkpoint comparison addressing training-data fit, extensions to all LoRA module types, and direct fine-tuning experiments supporting the observed layer-depth trend. Detailed per-attack results and search pseudocode improve transparency.
weaknesses: The central proxy interpretation is insufficiently validated. Classifying benign versus malicious prompts measures recognition of instruction content, not whether the model will refuse harmful requests. Likewise, robustness to zeroing half of a weight matrix need not predict robustness to small, learned LoRA updates. The paper does not establish a quantitative relationship between proxy changes and behavioral safety across candidate module subsets. Section 6.2 supports a depth trend, but does not validate the full proxy or the module-type and interaction claims.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of proxy-guided selection. In the general-domain experiments, the smaller learning rate is 10,000 times below the standard rate, effectively freezing much of the model. Necessary controls include uniformly reduced learning rates, simple late-layer tuning, and matched-size random module subsets, evaluated at comparable utility. The earlier-checkpoint comparison is helpful but does not replace these controls. Comparisons with existing safety-preserving fine-tuning methods are also absent.

The specific-domain evaluation explicitly selects checkpoints using test-set accuracy (Section 5.2), with different selection rules for standard IFT and ML-LR. A separate validation split and untouched test set are needed to substantiate capability preservation. The 100-example synthetic arithmetic task is also narrow evidence for the broader claims about domain expertise; general-domain utility decreases relative to the original models for both methods.

Evaluation independence and uncertainty need clarification. The proxy is trained and searched using AdvBench-derived examples, while AdvBench also appears in the final evaluation; disjointness is not documented. Automated attack prompts appear to come from an existing dataset, without a clear account of their target models or whether attacks are regenerated against the tuned models. No repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or human validation of the GPT-based judgments is reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful pseudocode and learning-rate details. The manuscript does not provide a code/data release statement, the manually edited proxy dataset, classifier training hyperparameters, or several fine-tuning and decoding settings. Algorithm 1 also assumes square attention matrices and attention-module access, leaving its implementation for non-square projections and the claimed all-module extension unclear.

Overall, the empirical reductions are promising, but the missing controls, unvalidated proxy interpretation, and test-based checkpoint selection leave important methodological questions unresolved. These warrant revision before a sound Findings recommendation; the concern is evidential adequacy rather than lack of interest in the problem.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: preserving safety alignment during task-specific instruction tuning. The proposed two-stage procedure is conceptually simple and applicable to standard LoRA training.

The reported benign-tuning results show substantial safety improvements while largely preserving measured task accuracy. For Llama2-7B on UltraInteract, SWAT reduces average ASR from 61.18% to 27.82% and harmfulness from 3.33 to 1.68, with task accuracy changing from 66.00% to 66.80%. Experiments cover three model families, two reasoning datasets, and several attack formats.

The paper provides useful exploratory evidence through cross-model-state probes, module perturbations, parameter-update measurements, and an instruction-modeling ablation. Reporting both refusal-based ASR and judged harmfulness is more informative than relying on either alone.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of classifier-guided module selection. SWAT adds 4 or 16 warm-up epochs and instruction modeling before the same 10-epoch IFT used by the baseline. Missing controls include matched-training-budget baselines, instruction modeling without selective warm-up, and equally sized random or simply late-layer module subsets. Table 7 establishes that instruction modeling contributes substantially, but does not establish that the proposed search is necessary. These comparisons are important to substantiate the central methodological contribution.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Reduced transfer accuracy of a benign/malicious classifier demonstrates a change in representations, but does not establish that this change causes unsafe generation; within-state classification remains nearly perfect. Likewise, robustness to removing half a weight matrix need not predict robustness to learned LoRA updates. Lower training loss without better task accuracy does not identify 'low-level features,' and smaller final parameter distances do not establish the proposed causal chain. The early-versus-late-layer experiment also lacks corresponding task-performance comparisons.

The probe evaluation is not independent of method selection: the nominal test representations are repeatedly used to search for modules, then used to support claims of preserved feature space. A separate held-out evaluation is needed. The paper also does not establish whether the AdvBench instructions used for probe construction overlap with downstream safety evaluation. Minimal lexical substitutions and only 100 training pairs leave the probe's generalization beyond this construction uncertain.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent. Classifier optimization, exact data selections, attack-data provenance, decoding settings, and baseline hyperparameters are insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 uses dLLM to halve every projection's rows, although grouped-query attention gives K/V projections different output dimensions; for the evaluated models this can yield whole-matrix or empty row perturbations. Its four-layer search increments also do not explain the two-layer boundaries shown for Qwen2 in Figure 4. The description of training 'all parameters' should distinguish full fine-tuning from updating all targeted LoRA adapters.

Claims of broadly successful integration with other defenses need qualification. Table 5 explicitly reports complete destruction of Llama3's language ability when both defenses are combined; adding Resta alone also worsens SWAT's average safety scores and task accuracy there. Under Attack IFT, SWAT's average ASR is 53.36%, compared with 38.70% for Safe LoRA, so its advantage is a safety–utility tradeoff rather than comparable safety across metrics. Missing standalone defense results on the other model families and combinations without SWAT further limit attribution.

Evaluation uncertainty and scope are inadequately characterized. There are no repeated runs or confidence intervals, despite small test sets and sub-percentage-point task differences. It is unclear whether automated attacks are regenerated against each defended model or evaluated as fixed transferred prompts. The stated 100 examples for manual attacks conflict with table percentages consistent with 110 examples. Refusal-string ASR can misclassify responses, and the GPT-4o judging setup is not sufficiently specified or validated. These issues, together with the missing controls and reproducibility gaps, prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present, although the promising empirical results justify revision for the next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: preserving safety alignment during downstream instruction tuning. The two-stage SWAT procedure is conceptually simple and compatible with LoRA.

The reported improvements over standard instruction tuning are substantial in several settings. For Llama2 on UltraInteract, average ASR falls from 61.18% to 27.82% and harmfulness from 3.33 to 1.68, while task accuracy remains comparable (66.00% versus 66.80%). Experiments cover three model families, two reasoning datasets, and both benign and contaminated training data, although coverage is uneven.

The paper includes useful supporting analyses: an instruction-modeling ablation, parameter-update measurements, early-versus-late-layer comparisons, and experiments combining SWAT with existing defenses. Reporting both refusal-based ASR and judge-based harmfulness provides complementary evidence.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of classifier-guided module selection. SWAT adds 4 or 16 warm-up epochs and instruction modeling before the same 10-epoch tuning stage. Missing controls include comparable warm-up using random or simply late-layer modules, instruction modeling without the proposed selection, and matched training budgets. Table 7 establishes that instruction modeling contributes substantially, but does not establish that the searched robust subset is necessary. These controls are central to assessing the proposed method rather than merely desirable extensions.

The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Reduced cross-model classifier accuracy demonstrates a change in representation coordinates, but does not establish that this change causes unsafe generation; each model's own classifier still separates benign and malicious instructions almost perfectly. Likewise, robustness to zeroing half a weight matrix is not established as a predictor of robustness to learned LoRA updates. Lower training loss without improved task accuracy does not demonstrate acquisition of 'low-level features.' The parameter-update analysis supports redistribution of updates, but not the full causal explanation.

The classifier evaluation lacks an independent final holdout. The 100 instruction pairs called test data are repeatedly used to select modules through classifier feedback, so subsequent performance on that set cannot independently validate preservation of the security feature space. The paper also does not establish disjointness between its AdvBench-derived selection data and downstream AdvBench evaluation. This leaves selection bias and possible benchmark overlap unresolved, without proving that the behavioral gains are artifacts.

Reproducibility is incomplete in consequential places. The manuscript omits classifier optimization details, important training and decoding settings, exact evaluation subsets, and sufficient information about attack generation and judge configuration. Appendix B provides examples rather than all test samples as claimed. Algorithm 1 also uses dLLM to split every projection's rows, which does not correctly express half-row pruning for the narrower K/V projections in grouped-query-attention models. The actual implementation needs clarification.

The broad claims about effectiveness and seamless combination need qualification. Under Attack IFT, standalone SWAT has worse average ASR than SafeLoRA (53.36% versus 38.70%), despite somewhat better task accuracy. On Qwen2, SWAT retains 55.87% average ASR and 90.91% SAP30 ASR. Table 5 reports complete destruction of language ability when both complementary defenses are added to SWAT on Llama3. Missing standalone defense results on the additional models and a defense-combination control without SWAT also limit attribution of the combined improvements.

Evaluation uncertainty is insufficiently characterized: there are no repeated runs or confidence intervals, task evaluation uses only 500 examples, and automated attacks use 50 examples each. Small task-accuracy differences therefore do not establish preservation or superiority reliably. The rule-based ASR can conflate refusal phrasing with safety, and it is unclear whether automated attacks were regenerated against each defended model. Together with the missing controls and reproducibility gaps, these issues warrant revision before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: preserving safety during downstream instruction fine-tuning. The proposed sequence of selective warm-up followed by broader LoRA tuning is practical and clearly motivated.

The reported improvements over standard fine-tuning are substantial. On Llama2 with UltraInteract, SWAT reduces average ASR from 61.18% to 27.82% and harmfulness from 3.33 to 1.68, while task accuracy changes from 66.00% to 66.80%.

Experiments span three model families, two reasoning datasets, benign and contaminated training settings, and multiple attack types. Reporting both refusal-based ASR and judged harmfulness provides useful complementary evidence.
The intermediate-model analysis, parameter-update measurements, and instruction-modeling ablation provide useful initial evidence about the method's behavior.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of classifier-guided module selection. SWAT adds 4 or 16 warm-up epochs and instruction modeling before the same 10-epoch IFT stage. Missing controls include matched-budget training, instruction modeling without selective warm-up, and warm-up on random or simply deep modules of comparable size. These are important for establishing the proposed selection method's value.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Cross-model probe transfer degradation demonstrates representation change, but does not establish that this change causes unsafe generation. Likewise, robustness to zeroing half a weight matrix need not predict robustness to LoRA updates. Reduced training loss without improved task accuracy does not establish learning of 'low-level features.'

Evaluation independence is insufficiently established. The classifier's nominal test representations are repeatedly used to select modules, making them validation data for that search. An untouched probe evaluation is needed. Because the probe data originate from AdvBench, overlap with the AdvBench safety evaluation should also be explicitly excluded.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the pseudocode and some hyperparameters. The manuscript does not adequately specify classifier optimization, exact data selections and splits, attack-generation budgets and whether attacks are regenerated for each defended model, decoding settings, or baseline tuning. Algorithm 1 also assumes square projection dimensions when splitting rows, which does not correctly describe the grouped-query K/V projections in Llama3 and Qwen2.

Several broad claims are contradicted or qualified by the results. Under Attack IFT, SWAT's average ASR is 53.36%, compared with 38.70% for SafeLoRA. Table 5 reports that combining both defenses completely destroys Llama3's language ability, contradicting seamless compatibility. Standalone baseline results for the other model families and defense combinations without SWAT are needed to assess comparative gains.

There are no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, making small task-accuracy differences difficult to interpret. The reported manual-attack sample counts also conflict with the percentage increments in the tables. These issues, together with the missing controls and reproducibility details, prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present; targeted revisions could reasonably address them next cycle.
